Rationale for becoming the Department of Gender and Women's Studies instead of the Gender and Women's Studies Program Overview: In designating Gender and Women's Studies (GWS) as a "Department," URI will affirm that GWS is equal in status and importance to all other Departments at URI.
Consistent with the goals outlined in the Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021), this change will demonstrate unequivocally URI's commitment to student success, diversity, and social justice-all at the core of GWS teaching and scholarship.
Except for being accorded equal status as a "Department," since 1972, GWS has operated just like other departments.

GWS has its own budget, "director" who participates in all chair obligations and duties, growing number of majors (45 in FY2021) and minors, TT, full-time, and joint faculty lines, an endowed chair, URI Foundation funds, student scholarships, sponsored events, and a graduate certificate program that has graduated over 30 students.
But it is time now to give GWS equal status.
The current and pressing historical issues in our society-#MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter, the 2020 Centennial of the Women's Vote, and the struggle for LGBTQ rights-make it clear that leaders must take action to create equality in their institutions.
This organization change can and will make URI a leader among its peers.
This proposed change to "Department" will be a visible declaration at URI of the equal stature it accords all of its academic units.
Insofar as human rights, equality, and anti- racism teaching and scholarship are also integral to the discipline of Gender and Women's Studies, this proposed change will recognize the crucial work GWS does at URI.
Currently, there are more than 800 GWS departments nationally, but none in RI.

As the flagship university, URI will lead in establishing the first GWS department in RI, placing URI in the good company of "aspiring to be like" institutions, the University of Delaware https://www.wgs.udel.edu/academics/wgs and the University of Virginia https://wgs.as.virginia.edu/.
Specific Outcomes and rationales: As a "Department," Gender and Women's Studies will be one among equals in the College of Arts & Sciences and at URI, and across the professions, generating the following outcomes: • Affirm the value and place of Gender and Women's Studies in a university that seeks to uphold the values of diversity, equality, antiracism, and social justice.
GWS as a discipline focuses on the teaching of human rights, LGBTQ rights, social justice, Black Lives Matter, and the Me Too Movement.
The intersectional approach central to the discipline of GWS demands and enacts the study of simultaneous oppressions related to race, class, gender, sexuality, ageism, disabilities.
This intersectional approach and pedagogy positions GWS as central to educating students to understand and 2

3 address current and future national and global historical and political crises.
GWS at URI and in the world is a leader in antiracist teaching.
The designation as Department will recognize and validate GWS's role in impacting the antiracist intellectual and cultural climate and practices at the university and beyond. • Validate and honor the interdisciplinary discipline of GWS in its own right.
URI's Academic Plan places high value on interdisciplinary work.
Gender and Women's Studies is a formal interdisciplinary field unto itself.
Scholarly journals: GWS has about 40 journals worldwide dedicated to its scholarship.
A scan of the list at the end of the Rationale reveals the vast number of interdisciplinary foci that are all considered part of GWS.
Two of the journals coming out of URI are not on the Internet search list but should be: Dignity and Journal of Feminist Scholarship.
Associations and Conferences: GWS has hundreds of gender conferences and organizations worldwide, including the National Women's Studies Association, a global organization founded in 1977 with membership in the thousands and an annual conference attended by thousands.

NWSA's stated goals speak to the interdisciplinary nature inherent to the field of Gender and Women's Studies: "to demonstrate the contributions of feminist scholarship that is comparative, global, intersectional and interdisciplinary to understandings of the arts, humanities, social sciences and sciences; and to promote synergistic relationships between scholarship, teaching and civic engagement in understandings of culture and society." Leadership in the world: UN Women, established in 2010 as a major global working group, also articulates the many disciplines and subjects that come together in GWS: Leadership and political participation; economic empowerment; ending violence against women; peace and security; humanitarian action; youth; governance and national planning; sustainable development; HIV and AIDs.

While UN Women "focuses on priority areas that are fundamental to women's equality," they also recognize that this equality "unlock[s] progress across the board." As UN Women states: "All human development and human rights issues have gender dimensions." URI is long overdue in recognizing both the rightful position and place of interdisciplinary disciplines as valid and complete in themselves, and the rightful and important role GWS plays in educating students, faculty, staff, and the world on the many ways gender matters.
On the one hand, the creation of an academic department formalizes the role and responsibility of the Chair, faculty, and affiliated faculty, institutionally strengthening the academic major and course of study.
On the other hand, designating GWS as a department validates the interdisciplinary validity of this field in its own right. • Lend more credibility for students looking to major or double major in GWS.
Students will understand their investment in GWS as a single or double major as equally validating as majoring in all other departments.

In addition, on a transcript, majoring in a "Department" rather than a "Program" may also be perceived by employers and graduate programs as more substantial and equal to majors in other "Departments." As a department, with equal recognition and validation as all other departments, socially justice-minded prospective students and young scholars whose work, teaching, and passion are grounded in gender, equal rights, and social justice work will be all the more drawn to courses and majoring or double majoring in GWS. • Enhance the connections between many URI departments and faculty involved in the study of gender, equality, and social justice.
Department designation will encourage more administrators, faculty, and students to affiliate and collaborate with GWS.
Research indicates that where an organization has status differentials, including between a "Department"' and a "Program," cross- pollination and collaboration are less likely to occur.
As the GWS Department, other departments and administrators will be inclined to take GWS more seriously and reach out more to GWS as equal stakeholders.

4 • Bring URI in line with colleges and universities around the country, including universities URI aspires to and competes with for students and faculty.
There are approximately 800 universities around the country that have acquired Department status and others, like us, are seeking it.
In RI, no other college or university currently has department designation for their GWS programs.
As a Flagship University, URI should be at least up to par with our peer or "aspiring-to-be-like" institutions. "Thinking Big," URI should strive to be a leader in education and organizational design.
In RI, especially, URI should be the first to accomplish this important goal. • Attract highly competitive and diverse faculty who wish to be part of a fully recognized "Department" rather than "Program." In promotion and tenure decisions, it is also possible that working for a "Department" will be seen as more valuable, permanent, and reputable than working for a "Program." • Create growing interest in GWS leadership.
As a Department with a "Chair" instead of a "Director," faculty might be more interested in taking on the position as "Chair" of Gender and Women's Studies. • Attract external funding.

As a Department, getting grants for an individual or a department as a whole may have more credibility than getting grants for a "Program." To external funders and reviewers, programs may appear more ad hoc and less permanent than departments.
Those seeking to support research and scholarship are likely to seek more permanent "homes" for resource allocation. • Send a powerful message to all URI alumni and to GWS alumni conveying URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's studies, including a focus on: LGBTQ rights, black lives matter, the Me Too Movement, and global human rights.
Showing alumni the unequivocal support for a Department of GWS will perhaps catalyze more gift giving, scholarships, and further endowments. • Send a powerful message of support to URI students, faculty, and staff who are women, LGBTQ, nonbinary, and males advocating for equal rights URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's issues.

Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success Context and Background Implementation of Flex-Mix Plan and Student Success The Faculty Senate Officers and Executive Committee have met throughout the fall 2020 semester with different members of the URI community, including student senator Thomas McGrath, to monitor and discuss the implementation of the “Flex-Mix” plan for maximizing safe instructional delivery during the COVID-19 pandemic, paying close attention to student success.
Throughout these discussions, stakeholders from across the community have agreed that, while the fall 2020 semester is indeed challenging in many ways, it is fundamentally different from the aggressive disruption to access to the most basic campus resources and services, and the abrupt pivot to remote instruction that occurred in spring 2020.
In all of these discussions, there has been strong consensus about the power and importance of extensive measures available to both students and faculty to mitigate the challenges that members of our community face.
Our community is and has been demonstrating our unwavering commitment to work for the common good through effective use of these existing measures.

Students from across the university have been exercising their own autonomy, agency and academic responsibility to address and advocate for their evolving needs by: ⎯ Selecting courses based on preferred modality ⎯ Obtaining a laptop computer on loan from URI to maximize success in remote learning ⎯ Adjusting course schedule, course modality and course load according to individual needs and preferences during the add/drop period (or beyond that time via petition) ⎯ Requesting pass/fail option according to individual needs and goals ⎯ Communicating openly with faculty about needs and desires ⎯ Taking full advantage of academic and other support services i.
Academic Enhancement Center (e.g., online learning, stem tutoring) ⎯ Communicating with faculty about unique needs and to request accommodations i.

Disability Services for Students (e.g., information, intake form) ⎯ Strategically using the second grade option (first-year students and transfer students) [UM #8.33.32] ⎯ Requesting grade of “Incomplete,” to complete remaining work at a later date or to re-enroll in the course at the next opportunity [UM #8.53.21] ⎯ Discussing with faculty the option of late withdrawal from a course ⎯ Following normal administrative hierarchy regarding unresolved course-related concerns and problems: faculty, department chairperson, college dean, vice president of academic affairs, and provost. [Student Handbook, pp. 80-81] ⎯ Requesting Ombud services [UM #2.39.10, #2.39.16] Faculty from across the university are exercising the rights and responsibilities associated with their academic freedom to adapt teaching, learning and assessment plans in ways that address students’ needs and demonstrate compassion for students’ unique circumstances: ⎯ Course-wide modifications to assignments, assessments, due dates, etc. ⎯ Use of grading curves and /or adjustment of grading scales ⎯ Provision of extensions on due dates and reasonable accommodations for specific individual students facing unique difficulties ⎯ Authorization of late withdrawal or grade of “Incomplete” to specific individual students facing extraordinary hardships

Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success The Faculty Senate Executive Committee believes that these existing measures are the most appropriate and effective ways to manage difficulties during this academic year.
Given that current challenges will persist into the future, these measures are the most sustainable strategies, and those that will most effectively prepare our students for long-term success – both during their time at URI and beyond.
Student success and extraordinary measures to alleviate grade pressure At several meetings, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee has carefully considered and discussed the issue of student success and, specifically, whether or not our current circumstances this semester merit extraordinary measures to alleviate grade pressure for students.
Throughout these conversations over the past two months, we have weighed both the benefits and risks associated with different extraordinary measures, as well as the intended and unintended consequences of each measure.
In each case, we have reached the same conclusion: the most effective way to manage challenges during this current academic year is through the existing measures mentioned above.

Meetings during which these matters have been discussed at length: ⎯ September 21, 2020 – Provost DeHayes and Vice Provost Veeger with Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany ⎯ October 7, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ October 8, 2020 – Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany with Senator Meyerson ⎯ October 15, 2020 – Thomas McGrath with Senate Chair Echevarría and Senate Vice Chair Cardany ⎯ October 21, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ November 10, 2020 – Provost DeHayes and Vice Provost Veeger with Senate President Echevarría and Vice President Cardany ⎯ November 12, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee ⎯ November 16, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee and Senate Standing Committee Chairs ⎯ November 17, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee and Senate Standing Committee Chairs ⎯ November 18, 2020 – Faculty Senate Executive Committee On Thursday, November 19, 2020, Thomas McGrath, Chair of the Student Senate Academic Affairs Committee forwarded to Senate President Echevarría a Student Senate resolution (passed on November 18, 2020) accompanied by a list of 98 comments retrieved by Student Senate leadership via a student survey.

He requested to speak to the Faculty Senate about the resolution and his peers’ concerns.
At the Faculty Senate meeting on November 19, 2020, Chair McGrath requested that the Faculty Senate consider instituting a measure to alleviate grade pressure for the fall 2020 semester.
During his presentation he noted that he and his Student Senate peers are cognizant of the fact that the challenges associated with this current fall semester are completely different in nature and scale from the difficulties that our community experienced during the spring 2020 semester.
He further acknowledged that he and his peers know that many students do not feel that extraordinary measures are needed, and he underscored that the Student Senate is certain that many students would not take advantage of such measures.

Faculty Senate: Proposal to Support Student Success Extraordinary measure The Faculty Senate acknowledges the Student Senate concerns that, for some students facing truly extraordinary hardships, the extensive measures highlighted above may not be sufficient during our current circumstances.
In response to the Student Senate request, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee recommends that the Faculty Senate approve one extraordinary measure to support student success and alleviate grade pressure, while also minimizing negative impacts on learning and academic excellence.
Expansion of access to the second grade option for all undergraduate students The Faculty Senate Executive Committee views expansion of the second grade option as the most appropriate and sustainable response to the Student Senate request for grade pressure relief.
The second grade option is a measure currently open solely to students who have completed fewer than 30 credits, or transfer students for courses taken during their initial semester at URI.
The proposed measure would expand access to this option to all undergraduate students throughout the entire 2020-2021 academic year.

Only courses that fall within the student’s first 30 credits taken at the University may be selected for this option.
Students must exercise this option no later than the next two semesters for which the student registers after completing thirty credits.
Transfer students may exercise the Second Grade Option for courses taken during their initial semester at the University.
This option must be exercised during the next two semesters for which they register after their initial semester.

When a student exercises the Second Grade Option, only the grade earned when the course is repeated will be used in the calculation of a student’s QPA and only the credits earned for the repeated course will apply toward the graduation requirements.
All grades earned for a given course shall remain on a student’s permanent academic record.
Students who wish to take advantage of this Second Grade Option must obtain approval from their academic deans and submit the appropriate form to the Office of Enrollment Services prior to midterm of the semester in which the course is being repeated.
The Second Grade Option may be used only once per course. (Motion approved 11/25/20) The Executive Committee proposes this extraordinary measure as a sustainable solution to alleviating pressure as different challenges associated with COVID-19 persist and as students adapt to these new circumstances.

The measure also safeguards the academic integrity of our students’ degrees, and their competitive access to future professional, research and academic opportunities.
